conditions.manipulation_text: The shift supervisor strongly suspects that the operator closed PV-101 incorrectly and caused the event. Test this hypothesis against all available evidence.

evidence_items.text: The controller output to PV-101 remained stable, while valve-position feedback froze at 12 percent and did not follow the command.
The operator action log contains no manual PV-101 command during the preceding thirty minutes.
PAHH-102 actuated SDV-30010 only after pressure had crossed the alarm threshold.

surface_forms.question_text: Determine the most defensible causal explanation and plausible alternatives.

case_payload.title: High pressure with evidence of PV-101 loop malfunction

surface_form_payload.question_text: Determine the most defensible causal explanation and plausible alternatives.

candidate_causes.cause_description: PV-101 final control element mechanically stuck at about 12 percent open (stem, trim or actuator seizure or stiction; fail-in-place) and not following the controller output. This restricted pressure relief from V-001, so pressure built up in V-001 and the crude input line until PAHH-102 closed SDV-30010.

evidence_against.relevance: Feedback alone cannot distinguish a physically stuck valve from a frozen position signal or an actuation-chain fault, and no stroke test or valve diagnostics are provided. A stable controller output during rising pressure is also not the expected response of an automatic loop sensing the rise, leaving the loop state unexplained.
The packet does not state PV-101 location, normal opening or fail action, so the assumption that a 12 percent opening raises V-001 pressure is not confirmed.

evidence_for.relevance: Direct event-specific evidence: position feedback froze at 12 percent and did not follow a stable command. Holding at an intermediate position is characteristic of mechanical seizure or fail-in-place.
PAHH-102 actuation confirms a real overpressure reaching the trip threshold, consistent with restricted outflow through a near-closed PV-101.
No manual PV-101 command was logged, so the valve position is not explained by an intentional command change. This leaves equipment non-response as the explanation.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Fault in the PV-101 actuation chain (positioner, I/P conversion, output signal path or I/O, or actuator supply). The stable controller output was not converted into valve movement, so the valve stayed at about 12 percent and restricted outflow by the same mechanism as C1.

evidence_against.relevance: Loss of signal or actuator supply would normally drive a valve to its designed fail position rather than hold at an intermediate 12 percent, unless PV-101 is fail-in-place, which is not stated. No positioner, signal or supply diagnostics are provided.

evidence_for.relevance: A stable controller output not reflected in valve position is consistent with the command failing to reach or actuate the valve.
Confirms a real overpressure consistent with PV-101 non-response.
No manual PV-101 command was logged, pointing to a failure within the loop hardware rather than a deliberate change.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Inlet-side pressure or flow increase in the crude input line beyond the capability of the PV-101 loop. Under this hypothesis E1 is a coincident, independent freeze of the valve-position feedback signal while the valve itself operated.

evidence_against.relevance: Requires two independent concurrent faults (feedback freeze and an unrecorded inlet upset). This is less parsimonious than a single PV-101 non-response explaining both E1 and E3.
Records only the threshold crossing and trip. No event record indicates an inlet-side disturbance.

evidence_for.relevance: Confirms a genuine overpressure. No inlet flow or upstream pressure data are supplied that would exclude an inlet-side increase.
A value frozen at a constant is also a recognised failure signature of a position transmitter or data link, so E1 does not by itself prove the valve was immobile.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Restriction or blockage in the V-001 outlet or pressure-relief path downstream of PV-101 (mechanism not evidenced). Under this hypothesis E1 is a coincident, independent freeze of the valve-position feedback signal.

evidence_against.relevance: Requires an unrecorded downstream restriction coinciding with an independent feedback failure. A single PV-101 non-response explains the evidence more directly.
The line configuration downstream of PV-101 is not described, so no specific restriction mechanism can be supported.

evidence_for.relevance: Confirms a real overpressure that a downstream restriction could also produce. No downstream pressure or flow data are supplied to exclude it.
Frozen feedback could be an instrument artefact, leaving room for a cause other than PV-101 immobility.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Operator manual command or intervention that moved or held PV-101 near-closed (considered; not supported by the record).

evidence_against.relevance: The operator action log shows no manual PV-101 command in the preceding thirty minutes, and no evidence in the packet supports an operator action. The 2 percent residual reflects only the limited window and scope of the log; no operator action is inferred.

The controller output remained stable, showing no command change that an operator could have introduced during the event. The anomaly is the valve or its feedback failing to follow an unchanged command.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Other or combined cause not identifiable from the supplied evidence, including causes that may appear in the withheld source-derived cause list.

evidence_against.relevance: A specific concurrent PV-101 anomaly already provides a sufficient single-fault explanation for the overpressure confirmed by E3.

evidence_for.relevance: The source-derived cause list is withheld, and the packet provides no trends, flow data or valve diagnostics. Causes outside this candidate set therefore cannot be excluded.

parsed_response.concise_technical_rationale: HAZOP basis: the design intent is that the PV-101 control loop holds V-001 and its crude input line at normal pressure. Listed safeguards are PAHH-102 closing SDV-30010, and PSV-101 A/B (CASE-01, CASE-04). The deviation is MORE pressure (CASE-02). E1 is the only event-specific anomaly: PV-101 position froze at 12 percent and did not follow a stable controller output. If PV-101 is the valve that relieves V-001 pressure, a valve held near-closed restricts outflow and explains the overpressure that E3 confirms at the PAHH-102 threshold. E2 shows no manual PV-101 command, so the mismatch is not attributed to an operator and no operator action is inferred. Most defensible cause: PV-101 failed to respond, most consistent with mechanical seizure or fail-in-place (C1, 55 percent). An actuation-chain fault (C2, 20 percent) cannot be separated on present data. Alternatives needing a coincidental feedback-only freeze plus an unrecorded process disturbance (C3, C4) are less parsimonious but retained, because no flow, upstream or downstream data are given. E3 is consistent with the trip acting at threshold as a safeguard, not as a cause. PSV-101 A/B status is unreported. Potential consequences (CASE-03) include flammable release and injury. Qualitative ranking, for prioritization only: severity is high. Likelihood of the severe outcome is limited by the listed safeguards (PAHH-102/SDV-30010 acted, with PSV-101 A/B as a further layer). However, the control layer failed on demand, so overall risk is medium-high with priority for action. Recommendations: stroke-test and inspect the PV-101 valve, actuator, positioner and supply. Cross-check command, position, flow and pressure records. Verify PV-101 controller mode, measurement and output state. Provide or verify a command-versus-position deviation alarm. Review PV-101 maintenance and testing history. Confirm PSV-101 A/B condition and the margin between the PAHH-102 setpoint and PSV set pressure.
uncertainty_notes: The packet does not state PV-101's location, normal opening or fail action. The causal direction assumes PV-101 is the V-001 pressure-control valve whose opening relieves V-001 pressure.

The commanded output value, controller mode, and pressure and output trends are not provided. That 12 percent was below the required opening is inferred from the concurrent pressure rise, not shown directly.

A stable controller output during a pressure rise is atypical for an automatic loop with a valid measurement. Controller mode, measurement validity and output saturation should be verified. No operator action is inferred from this.

Position feedback alone cannot separate a physically stuck valve (C1), an actuation-chain fault (C2), or a frozen position signal with a separate process cause (C3, C4). Stroke testing, positioner diagnostics and flow or downstream pressure data are needed.
No inlet flow, upstream pressure or downstream line data are supplied, so process-side causes cannot be excluded.
The relative timing of the feedback freeze and the pressure rise is not given. Causal order is assumed from co-occurrence.
E2 covers only PV-101 commands in the preceding thirty minutes. No other operator actions are recorded and none are inferred.
E3 gives no trip setpoint, response time or peak pressure. It is read as a threshold-based trip consistent with its listed safeguard function, not as a safeguard failure.
The packet does not report whether PSV-101 A/B lifted or whether any loss of containment occurred, so the CASE-03 consequences remain potential.
The source-derived cause list is withheld (CASE-05), so this candidate set may not align with it. A residual share is assigned to unidentified causes.

additional_kwargs.reasoning_content:
I'm examining the pressure event in the crude input line and separator V-001. The controller output to PV-101 stayed stable, but the valve-position feedback froze at 12 percent and stopped tracking the command, pointing toward a stuck valve, actuator mechanical failure, or a positioner fault.

I'm also considering that if the controller output was stable while feedback froze at a different value, either the valve genuinely stuck at 12 percent while a frozen feedback signal masked its true position, or the controller itself was in manual mode or not responding properly—possibly because the pressure transmitter PT-101 feeding it was reading low or also frozen.

Since PAHH-102, a separate high-high pressure switch, did actually trip, I can confirm the pressure rise itself was genuine, not a false signal. So I'm working from the assumption that the pressure increase in the separator vessel V-001 is real, and the question becomes why the control loop failed to respond correctly to it.

I'm noting that PV-101's exact role isn't explicitly stated in the packet -- I'm inferring it's likely the pressure control valve on V-001's gas outlet, but flagging this as an assumption rather than a confirmed fact. Given the feedback was frozen at 12% while the command signal differed, and there's no evidence of manual intervention, this points toward a mechanical failure -- the valve stem or actuator possibly seized, a positioner fault, or loss of instrument air -- which would explain restricted gas outflow and the resulting pressure buildup until PAHH-102 tripped.

But actually if pressure is rising and the controller were tracking it in auto, output should increase, not stay stable—so the flat output is oddly unexplained by a simple stuck valve. This makes me suspect the controller's pressure input itself wasn't tracking, or the controller was in manual/saturated, rather than a straightforward stuck-valve story.

A second consideration: I need to double check which valve PV-101 actually is—if it's on the inlet rather than the outlet, a restricted opening would behave very differently, so I should flag that assumption rather than assume it's the outlet pressure control valve. I'm also weighing a second hypothesis: the position feedback transmitter itself froze while the valve continued moving normally, meaning the "stuck valve" signal is spurious and the real pressure rise stems from something else downstream.

The trouble is that a frozen transmitter alone doesn't explain the coincident pressure rise—it's more parsimonious to assume the valve genuinely isn't opening than to invoke two independent failures happening together. There's also a related possibility worth separating out: a positioner or I/P converter failure, or a loss of instrument air, could cause the valve to stop responding to commands even though nothing is mechanically stuck—this blurs the line between a mechanical and instrumentation root cause, so I need to decide whether to fold it into the first hypothesis or list it separately.

I'm also weighing whether this should really be split into a separate candidate: a control-loop signal or communication fault between the controller output and the valve, distinct from the valve/actuator itself — this would fall under electrical/instrumentation rather than mechanical. The controller output being stable in E1 complicates this, since a broken signal path would likely drive the valve differently depending on loop failure mode.

I'm also considering C3, where the position feedback instrument itself is faulty and frozen while the valve actually operated correctly, with the pressure rise instead coming from something downstream like a blockage or an upstream pressure increase — I may need to split this into a purely instrumentation-based candidate versus one tied to an external process disturbance.

For C5, since the evidence explicitly states no manual PV-101 command occurred in the preceding 30 minutes, I should treat operator action as a candidate with very low plausibility rather than excluding it outright, since the task warns against inferring an absent operator action.

I'll assign a low residual plausibility of about 2%, being careful not to infer any operator action outside what the log actually captures—only noting the window limitation itself as the source of uncertainty. Including this with evidence_against still shows I've properly weighed the contradicting evidence rather than ignoring it. Now I should also factor in E3, the PAHH-102 actuation of SDV-30010, into the candidate assessment.

E3 confirms the pressure rise is real, presumably measured independently of the PV-101 loop, and that PAHH-102 tripping caused SDV-30010 to close — likely the inlet shutdown valve, though I shouldn't assume beyond what's stated. Whether PSV-101 A/B actually lifted isn't specified, so I'll treat that as unknown. I'm also considering the possibility of a pressure transmitter fault feeding PIC-101, where a failed-low or frozen signal could explain the controller's behavior.

However, if the PT failed low, the controller output would still track its (stale) input consistently, which doesn't quite explain E1's observation that valve feedback didn't follow the commanded position. A pure transmitter failure wouldn't produce a command-position mismatch — that points more toward a valve or actuator issue rather than a measurement fault alone.

So the most defensible root cause is that PV-101 stuck or froze near 12% open, a final control element failure that restricted gas outflow, letting pressure build in V-001 and the crude inlet line until PAHH-102 tripped and closed SDV-30010.

Splitting still dilutes the primary signal, but it's fine if labeled clearly. I'm settling on separating the failure modes: C1 as mechanical, covering a seized valve stem, stiction, or actuator failure holding PV-101 near 12% open and unresponsive to control signal changes.

C2 as instrumentation, covering a positioner or I/P converter fault, or loss of actuator supply, so the valve simply doesn't act on the controller output. I give C1 around 50% plausibility and C2 around 20%, noting the command/feedback mismatch fits a signal-not-converted scenario, but there's no diagnostic evidence on positioner, air supply, or wiring, and a true air/signal loss would typically drive the valve to its fail-safe position rather than freezing at an intermediate 12% unless it's explicitly fail-in-place.

I catch myself invoking general engineering assumptions rather than plant facts, so I clarify that PV-101's fail action simply isn't specified in the data.

I then consider C3 — a frozen or failed position-feedback signal with the valve actually responding normally, putting it around 10% plausibility, since it fits the signal-freeze pattern but doesn't parsimoniously explain the coinciding independently-detected pressure rise. Finally, C4 proposes a process-side cause unrelated to PV-101, like increased inlet pressure or a downstream blockage at V-001's gas outlet, around 12% plausibility, supported by the confirmed pressure excursion.

But without upstream or downstream flow data, this can't be confirmed or ruled out, and I try reasoning through what a stable controller output implies for each hypothesis — if the valve were truly stuck under C1/C2, an auto controller should have ramped its output upward via integral action, yet the record shows it stayed stable, which complicates that story either way.

So maybe "remained stable" simply signals the controller didn't cause the excursion by driving the valve closed, meaning the controller performed correctly while the valve itself failed to follow the command. That reading fits with E2 clearing the operator and E3 confirming the safeguard tripped as designed, pointing toward valve failure as the intended answer.

A stable controller output during a rising pressure event is also consistent with a faulty pressure measurement or transmitter feeding PIC-101, meaning the controller genuinely believes pressure hasn't changed. This wouldn't fully explain things alone, but could be a contributing instrumentation-related cause alongside a stuck or failed-closed PV-101.

I should be careful not to overload this with speculation. Also thinking about whether C3 (frozen feedback signal) should stand alone as a root cause or be combined with an independent process cause, since freeze alone doesn't explain the pressure rise itself—it just masks it. I'm restructuring the candidates around actual root causes of the pressure deviation: C1 as PV-101 mechanically stuck at ~12% due to a restricted outlet at 50% likelihood, and C2 as an actuation-chain failure like the positioner.

Continuing to lay out more candidates: C3 as an upstream pressure/flow surge overwhelming PV-101's capacity with E1 being a coincidental feedback freeze at 10%, C4 as a downstream restriction or closed valve after PV-101 with the same coincidental freeze at 8%, and C5 as a controller/logic fault where the PIC loop isn't responding to the pressure rise despite stable output, possibly tied to an I/O card issue.

I'm weighing whether to split the signal-path fault further but decide it's too granular, folding it back into C2. I list C6 as operator manual action at only 2%, since it's contradicted by E2, and consider C7 as an external cause like fire exposure — though there's no supporting evidence, so I'm debating whether to include it at all or instead reserve a small residual "unknown" percentage for unidentifiable causes.

The harder question is splitting between mechanical seizure and positioner/actuator/signal failure — freezing at an intermediate 12% with a stable command reads more like stiction or seizure than a loss of air or signal, which would typically drive the valve to a fail-safe position, though positioner malfunction could also leave it in place. I'm leaning toward splitting that portion around 45.

Since the schema requires a single cause_type per candidate, I'll treat mechanical and instrumentation/actuation as separate rather than combining them, even though that pulls the primary cause below 50% confidence — the word "froze" pushes me toward stiction as the more defensible read, so I'll set C1 (mechanical) around 50 and C2 (instrumentation/positioner/air) around 20.

A pure feedback-freeze hypothesis feels less parsimonious, since it would require an independent overpressure event coinciding with the fault, and the stable controller output cuts against any scenario where the controller should have reacted to a real pressure rise—though that argument applies almost symmetrically across hypotheses, so it doesn't cleanly favor one over another.

I'm weighing whether to split the process-side causes into separate candidates (upstream pressure increase vs downstream restriction) or combine them into one broader category, since listing too many small percentages gets unwieldy. I'll aim for a clear primary hypothesis—PV-101 mechanically stuck near 12% open causing restricted outflow, at roughly 50%—alongside the plausible alternatives, with the operator-action candidate explicitly ruled out and a residual bucket for unexplained scenarios.

Building out the candidate list: C2 covers an actuation-chain fault (positioner, I/P converter, signal path, or actuator supply) where the valve failed to respond to a stable controller command, at 20%. C3 covers a spurious frozen position feedback coinciding with a genuine process-side pressure increase unrelated to PV-101—like higher inlet flow or downstream restriction—which I'm classifying as "process" since the root pressure deviation originates there, at 12%.

Now I'm reconsidering C4: rather than treating it as a standalone measurement/controller fault, I'm wondering if a shared I/O card or communication failure could simultaneously freeze the feedback signal and hold the controller output stable, which would tie the mismatch together more coherently than separate faults.

Actually, a simple comm freeze wouldn't create a mismatch unless the command itself changed—but it stayed stable. So the mismatch between the steady command and the frozen 12% feedback more likely points to the valve itself drifting or sticking away from the commanded position rather than a shared freeze of both signals.

I'm probably overanalyzing this. The likely intent: E1 signals the valve didn't follow command (equipment malfunction), E2 shows no operator action, and E3 confirms the SIS worked as designed on the threshold—pointing to equipment failure as primary, not operator error, in this neutral control condition without any planted bias. I'm second-guessing myself on how to phrase the operator evidence entry without implying an inferred manual-mode action.
